questions.question: Why does an AI portfolio need active management?
options: Because every pilot that produced a working demo should be scaled into production
Because quick wins, strategic bets, risk controls, capacity, and learning need balancing
Because measuring initiatives slows delivery, so the review cadence should stay light
Because ownership can be assigned later, once the strongest initiative has emerged
questions.explanation: Portfolio management makes tradeoffs visible across initiatives. Not every pilot should scale, and without portfolio discipline teams overcommit while weak pilots keep running.

questions.question: Six AI initiatives are running and all of them look promising. What does this lesson say is missing?
options: A shared delivery platform so the six teams stop building the same components twice
A single executive sponsor who can approve budget for all six without further review
A communications plan so the organisation hears about each initiative at the right time
A way to compare value, dependency, risk, staffing, and evidence across the whole set
questions.explanation: The lesson's problem is comparability: each initiative looks promising, but nobody can weigh value, dependency, risk, staffing, and evidence on the same terms. Portfolio management turns scattered initiatives into a managed set of bets.

questions.question: What does the Python artifact produce?
options: A ranked portfolio plan with matched controls and rationale per initiative
A strategy deck generated from the scored initiatives for the steering meeting
A production deployment of whichever initiative scored highest in the cycle
A guaranteed business case for each initiative that finance can sign off on
questions.explanation: The artifact supports portfolio triage and steering by ranking initiatives and matching controls to each one.

questions.question: Which control belongs to this lesson?
options: A capacity assumption that every team can absorb one more initiative
A review cadence that is set once the roadmap has already been agreed
Kill criteria that say in advance when an initiative is paused or stopped
A dependency list kept inside each team rather than on the portfolio board
questions.explanation: Kill criteria help teams stop weak initiatives before they become zombies. The portfolio board, review cadence, and scaling decision are the other controls this lesson teaches.

questions.question: When should an initiative receive stronger portfolio controls?
options: Only after the initiative has already shipped and is running in production
Only when no business stakeholder has been attached to the initiative
When impact, uncertainty, dependencies, or capacity conflicts are high
Only when the initiative appears on more than one team's roadmap at once
questions.explanation: High-risk portfolio items need explicit review and steering. The score combines impact, uncertainty, dependency, and capacity rather than any single trigger.

questions.question: Why are kill criteria useful?
options: They stop weak pilots from consuming team capacity indefinitely
They let a paused initiative restart without a new business case
They replace the review cadence with a single end-of-cycle decision
They set the scaling threshold that every successful pilot must clear
questions.explanation: Kill criteria protect capacity and focus, keeping zombie initiatives from crowding out the rest of the portfolio.
